quotes.text: Policy is the law. Tags are the context. Logic apps are the action. That distinction matters because most governance designs fail by mixing all three together.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Condenses the whole cleanup-engine architecture into three clearly separated roles.

quotes.text: The sequence of how you roll this out is everything. Audit first, then modify, then deny.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Gives a concrete, repeatable rollout order for Azure Policy enforcement.

quotes.text: Age tells you the duration, but it doesn't tell you the intent. Expiry date tells you the intent, or TTL does.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains why expiry tags beat resource age as a deletion signal.

quotes.text: Deletion only feels dangerous when the context is weak. Strong tags turn cleanup from a risky guess into a controlled decision.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Reframes automated deletion as a data-quality problem rather than a risk problem.

quotes.text: Stop treating cloud waste like a reporting issue, start treating it like a life cycle control issue
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: States the central mindset shift of the episode in one sentence.

takeaways: Split the cleanup engine into three layers: Azure Policy sets the rules, tags carry the lifecycle context, and Logic Apps take the action.
Keep a small, standardized tag set (owner, environment, cost center, expiry, cleanup action, exception reason) and roll out policy in the order audit, modify, then deny.
Check locks, dependencies and soft-delete behavior before deleting, start with low-risk classes like unattached disks in dry-run mode, and track both reclaimed and prevented cost.
hook: Most Azure bills are inflated by idle VMs, orphaned disks and forgotten sandboxes that nobody owns anymore. This episode shows cloud and platform teams how to combine Azure Policy, tags, Resource Graph and Logic Apps into an automated cleanup engine that removes waste safely and keeps it from coming back.
